quotes.text: this turbulence modeling approach primarily relies on the use of wall models (also known as wall functions) to capture the flow behavior near the walls and avoid excessive mesh refinement

In particular, the boundary conditions for νt (nutWakeFunctions) were designed to produce the same wall shear stress that is predicted by the wall and wake laws, while the alphatWakeFunctions for αt aim to preserve the heat flux at the walls.

wall functions are implemented to circumvent an excessive mesh refinement on the wall by allowing the placement of the first computational node in the logarithmic region, thus avoiding a complete integration towards the wall.

independently_located_designs.source_reading: Each k–epsilon member is tested with both scalable and Menter–Lechner; within each family the selected mesh is held for the final comparison. Mesh selection uses pressure drop/outlet temperature for one member; different families can select different meshes. In the two passages the pressure drop is a free observable and no differential pressure was prescribed. The applied inlet velocity, temperatures and inlet development are separate. Retain correlation choice: Rothfus-corrected Colebrook, Serth and Sinnot differ; the authors report up to 24% between two outer pressure-drop correlations. Heat-transfer U is separate.
independently_located_designs.scientific_effect: Matched intra-closure wall-treatment contrast on pressure drop. Comparing different closures/meshes or picking a different empirical correlation changes the question.

quotes.text: Wall boundary conditions for Lattice Boltzmann simulations of turbulent flows with wall functions
Keywords: Lattice Boltzmann Method, Boundary condition, wall model, wall function, Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes

Since standard LBM relies on isotropic Cartesian grids, resolving turbulent boundary layers at high Reynolds numbers demands extremely fine meshes, making those simulations computationally expensive or impractical. To address this issue, wall functions are widely used in both RANS and WMLES-based LBM simulations.

records.reason: Disposition contested, by clarification S3. The diffuser LES is a whole calculation with an identifiable wall treatment that the source itself calls wall modelling (Sec. 2.3, Eq. 6), so the method is inside the paper-level rule; but its only comparison with a comparator is a statement, and the channel comparison is announced without any displayed or quoted value, so neither design qualifies, and the paper has no other qualifying design (the periodic-pipe comparison of two domain lengths has no comparator and no stated wall treatment). The published rule alone does not say whether a statement-only comparison is a 'source-located comparison'; S3 settles it as contested (second reading). Group coupled_wmles: both readings describe the diffuser LES and the channel validation with the same facts; membership follows the disposition, so under S3 no design enters coupled_wmles as a qualifying design. The sublayer point (first cell required inside the viscous sublayer) does not change the disposition: the wall-treatment definition of rules_v2 is not the paper-level rule.

The source compares these choices at the named test conditions. Fig. 7 includes prescribed LS89 wall stress and heat flux as well as two isothermal cases. At LS89, Sigma and Smagorinsky produce different suction-side transition, directly affecting shear (Fig. 13 vs 14).
independently_located_designs.scientific_effect: Separate the SC2/SC3 exposure and property change, prescribed versus coupled LS89, and mechanical versus thermal endpoints. A claim for the winner selected on these held-out runs differs from an evaluation of both trained models as prespecified. Thermal evidence cannot stand for shear. Turbine shock transition is outside the main smooth low-Mach stratum.

quotes.text: We present a novel approach to hybrid RANS/LES wall modeling based on function enrichment, which overcomes the common problem of the RANS–LES transition and enables coarse meshes near the boundary.

The velocity gradient is resolved, although the first off-wall node for the LES may be placed in a range 𝑦+1 ∼ 1 … 100, which is possible due to the interaction of the RANS and LES scales and due to the use of a tailored spatial discretization via function enrichment.

The key idea is to construct the shape functions by using a wall-law as an enrichment function, which enables the resolution of the high velocity gradient at the no-slip boundary with very few degrees of freedom.

The published rule alone does not decide. Method words: forecasting models / CNN models; returns the future wall-shear-stress field; no coupled calculation and no first-cell spacing. No fact is disputed between the readings.

quotes.text: To explore the practical implications of these interactions, we train three additional convolutional neural network (CNN) models to predict the future wall-shear stress τx (x∥ , t+∆T ) using the past streamwise velocity fluctuations as input.

The leftmost panel shows the ground-truth target field obtained from DNS. The second and third panels show CNN predictions using only u1 and only u2 , with corresponding relative mean-squared errors (RMSE) of 0.21 and 0.83, respectively.

which achieve RMSE values of 0.21, 0.83, and 0.21, respectively. The best performance is obtained using only the near-wall input u1 , consistent with its strong unique causal contribution identified in the SURD analysis.
where τ̂x and τxDNS represent the predicted and reference wall-shear stress fields, respectively, and ⟨·⟩x,z,t denotes the average over all spatial locations (x, z) and time snapshots t.
The simulation is driven by a constant streamwise mass flux and fully resolves all spatial and temporal turbulence scales.

Fig. 4 compares flat-plate velocity, eddy-viscosity, k and ω profiles against wall integration under varying matching points; increasing y+(1) also coarsens the mesh. Fig. 5 gives Cf×1000 on ZPG and a pressure-gradient-induced separation bubble versus x/L, matching-point curves 1.1,2.5,5,11,25,111. The author notes weaker sensitivity in recirculation. Captions contain neither an explicit newly generated run statement nor an attribution for these exact graphics. The text attributes the lookup-table method and more elaborate tests to Kalitzin et al.

disposition_settlement.reason: Disposition eligible under the published rule as written; no clarification is needed (classical wall function in a RANS whose first node lies at y+(1) up to 111; S3 is met by the plotted curves of Figs 4 and 5 against the wall-integrated solution). Method words: wall function (look-up table, Kalitzin et al 2005); returns boundary values of k and omega at the first node; first-node y+(1) = 2.5, 5, 11, 25, 111. The rule is silent on review provenance and does not make it a condition; the source does not state that Figs 4-5 are taken from another publication. Membership does not depend on the rough-wall conditions of Sec. 4, which the source applies to wall-integrated models. Fact: the source does not say whether the runs of Figs 4-5 are new (first reading correct).

quotes.text: The second topic of this review is the wall function. Analysis of flow in complex geometries can impose severe demands on mesh resolution. Wall functions are a firmly established method to reduce the demands on meshing.

Kalitzin et al (2005) advocate a method based on a look-up table. It is assumed that the turbulence model can be integrated with the wall on a fine grid, and the desire is to develop a technique to use coarse near-wall grids.
Then the portion lying within the universal layer is saved to create a table that can be interpolated to provide a boundary value at y+ (1).
That idea is tested in figure 4 for the k–ω model. The various curves are for the various y+ (1) values indicated in the legend. The solid curve is an accurate integration with the wall.
More elaborate testing (Kalitzin et al 2005) confirms the insensitivity to the matching point.
Figure 5 shows skin friction coefficients for two cases; the upper one is a flat plate and the lower one is a plate with pressure gradient-driven separation and reattachment.

disposition_settlement.reason: First-reading value kept. The third reading finds that the published paper-level rule does not decide whether a check of a wall model's internal mixing-length relation against DNS, with no wall stress evaluated, 'tests a named treatment'. Clarification S2 only says that the relation is not a stress estimator; it does not address that clause. The published rule set counts a paired observation that can exclude a stated restriction as an evidence type (constitutive constraint), which by definition evaluates no wall model. Under settlement_plan.md a fact the rule does not decide keeps its first-reading value; the work is marked as a scope-boundary work, so every count is also given without it.

independently_located_designs.source_location: Published §4.2, Eq. 23–24, Tables 4–5, Figs. 6–10. SGS and collision experiments in later subsections.
independently_located_designs.source_reading: Fixed MRT D3Q19 + Vreman and common periodic channel, geometries/averaging within each resolution. Eq. 23 has a feedback force involving mean bulk speed and average wall friction velocity. On the y+=25 grid, Reichardt→Musker relative profile L2 errors in Table 4 change from 0.01400 to 0.01553 for mean U, 0.3404 to 0.4199 for uu and 0.3592 to 0.3351 for uv. At y+=50, mean U goes from 0.04129 to 0.03731. Table 5 reports friction-velocity and Re errors plus cost on those runs.
independently_located_designs.scientific_effect: Add controlled-wall membership. Repeated y+ cases are distinct meshes and matched only within a row. The SGS study then chooses Musker using these results, and Table 9 changes collision scheme at fixed Musker.

independently_located_designs.source_reading: The Mach 6 disturbed laminar boundary layer with 4-degree oblique-shock impingement tests several reconstruction schemes and uses H2K/Sandham Stanton data. In the Mach 7.7 15-degree compression ramp, only MEG-C-CONS was run, with two resolutions; Fig. 12 compares both mean pressure coefficient and Stanton number to Cao/Roghelia DNS/experiment. Pressure shows slightly upstream separation. Intermediate density plots have no quantitative reference of the same field. Source discusses extended DNS Reynolds/ramp length.
independently_located_designs.scientific_effect: These are two different transitional hypersonic whole-calculation designs. Scalar/thermal agreement and visual density contours cannot substitute for the Fig. 12 hydrodynamic pressure reference.

the linear interpolation for the velocity at the IB nodes will lead to significant error of flow prediction, because the IB nodes do not fall inside the viscous sublayer

quotes.text: the high Reynolds number wall treatment method needs less computational capacity based on that, its required y+ range is between 30 and 300. While in the case of the low Reynolds wall treatment method the required y+ range is below 10, which could increase the cell count.
The two turbulence models are the widely used k-omega STT in vehicle aerodynamics and the k-ε realizable with the Enhanced Wall Treatment setting.

In the case of the low Reynolds number wall treatment method, the model uses wall functions to describe the flow near the walls, while in the case of high Reynolds number wall treatment method, the viscous sublayer is resolved (Kristóf, 2019).

quotes.text: In the proposed wall-modeling approach, hereafter referred to in this paper as wall mean-resolved LES (WMRLES), the boundary layer mesh is constructed such that pure LES is supported in the outer layer and hybrid RANS-LES is supported in the inner near-wall layer.
This approach eliminates the need for analytical or numerical wall functions to be applied at the wall boundary, at the expense of additional mesh resolution in the near-wall layer.

disposition_settlement.reason: (1) No relation supplies a wall stress or a wall boundary value. All wall-bounded runs sit on grids with y+(1) = 0.2 (1 for Fig. 10) with a no-slip wall (stated for the channel; not stated in words for the flat plate). The method is a hybrid RANS-LES whose RANS layer is integrated to the wall and which the source presents as wall-modelled LES, so the disposition is eligible under the published rule with clarification S1 (S3 is met by the quoted Re_tau values and the plotted profiles and c_f); without S1 the published rule does not decide it, which is the second reading's 'contested'. With eligibility the first reading's memberships apply (coupled_wmles; K01 strict, K02 broad, K04 strict). (2) Member contrasts, identical in both readings and supported by the source: K01 strict - arms: (a) differential SSG/LRR stress in the near-wall RANS layer blended by f_B (Eq. 11) against (b) Boussinesq stress also in that layer (Eq. 12, f_user = 0); variant_type different model; six factors fixed (one channel set-up; same eddy-viscosity sub-grid model, c_DES = 0.65, in the LES region; pair on the base mesh); reference_comparison tabulated (text: 4246/4289 against 4112/4135, DNS 4179; Figs 6 and 7 on common axes with DNS). K02 broad - variant (a), Re_delta = 98300, c_l = 5, 2.5, 40 at c_t = 1.87; same model, different parameter; factors fixed; plotted (Fig. 5 with DNS; legend Re_tau 4246, 4310, 4221); the c_t sweep listed as a fourth arm is a statement only and not a displayed arm. K04 strict - flat plate, (a) in Fig. 9a and (b) in Fig. 9b, each with the Coles-Fernholz correlation and its tolerance band on identical axes, both labelled y+(1) = 0.2; different model; factors fixed; plotted (the arms are in separate panels, as both readings note, but each is on the same scale as the reference, so 'plotted' and not 'qualitative' fits the rule). No factual error found in either reading on these rows; the readings differ only in the disposition and, on non-member row K05, in averaging (unreported against equal; the source states no averaging length for the SST-IDDES data).

quotes.text: Simulations of periodic channel flows at different Reynolds numbers and grid resolutions are used to calibrate and validate the wall-modelled LES branch of the new model.
The function fB , which is active for the WMLES branch, blends between the RANS mode for the inner turbulent boundary layer (fB = 1) and the LES mode for the outer boundary layer (fB = 0)
the wall-modelled LES (WMLES) branch of IDDES is addressed in this section.
Periodic boundary conditions are applied in streamwise as well as spanwise directions whereas no-slip wall conditions are present for the upper and lower face.

The spatial resolution in wall-normal (y) direction is characterised by a wall-adjacent grid spacing of y + (1) = 0.2 and a growth rate of r = 1.14 leading to 65 cells for Reδ = 6875 and 141 cells for Reδ = 98300.
To this end, the mesh resolution was increased by a factor of two in all spatial coordinate directions resulting in 130 x 282 x 130 cells in x, y and z, respectively.

Jet: interface at y*/D = 0.02 (H/D = 2) and 0.04 (H/D = 6), Re_y* 166 to 586 at the stagnation point; no y+ stated for the 120-cell log-law mesh. "the condition y* > yd is always satisfied". Wall condition: Robin conditions on U and k (Dirichlet on epsilon and V) at the interface for IBC; scalable log-law wall function for the comparator

quotes.text: A one-dimensional boundary layer equation is used to transfer the boundary conditions from the wall to an interface within the flow.
This approach avoids the computational expense of fully simulating the turbulent boundary layers.
The alternative is not to fully resolve the boundary layer. This is the approach taken by high Reynolds number (HRN) models, which typically utilise wall functions.

scope_boundary.basis: N372-D01 (mesh M2, spacing 3.60, Table V: 3) is S. new-1 (M1 to M4: 4.50, 3.60, 2.35, 1.65) is S. new-2 is S for nine of its eleven grids (G1 3, G2 4, G21 2, G31 1e-2, G32 7e-2, G33 3, G34 2, G41 2, M4 2); for G3 (6) and G4 (7) the question as written does not decide: the tabulated quantity is the cell height at the wall, so the first cell centre lies near 3 to 3.5 and the grid reaches the sublayer, but taken as a first-cell value 6 and 7 are above 5 and the clause "in every calculation" would then make new-2 U and the work M. Recorded here as S (work_class S) because no first cell lies above the sublayer; the alternative reading is new-2 U, work_class M. The Introduction sentence "y+ values from 4 to 11" conflicts with the tables and is not attached to any named grid.

quotes.text: To perform wall-modeled LES, different meshes have been generated, with y+ values from 4 to 11.
The van Driest wall-damping function is used in the wall treatment for the SMG and OEEVM subgrid models. Whereas, a wall-model is instead used for the WALE, DSEM, and LDKM models.

This wall model is based on the Spalding’s law of the wall from which the friction velocity can be estimated based on which a wall viscosity can be derived at the first off-wall grid point, following the ideas of [41].

independently_located_designs.scientific_effect: Group 2 supports a controlled intervention on target-informed idealized wall treatments, not independent wall-stress transfer. Group 1 cannot validate its imposed mean traction. Keep wall velocities and figures from each group separate.

independent_scope_reading.interpretation: The held-out non-sinusoidal waveforms test a whole-field time-series forecast of the two velocity components on a meridional plane. quotes.text: The spatiotemporal evolution of pulsating turbulent pipe flow was predicted by deep learning.

proposed a deep learning model utilizing a CNN LSTM architecture as a data-efficient surrogate model for the DNS of pulsating flows. The model predicts future flow fields based on the current spatial flow field and the pressure gradient information of the next time step.

quotes.text: In this study, the temporal evolution of flow fields in the r-z cross-section, obtained from DNS of pulsating turbulent pipe flow, is predicted using a deep learning approach. The input data consist of the streamwise velocity uz and the radial velocity ur defined on 96 × 256 grid points in the r-z plane.
quotes.location: Sec. 2.2.1 (input and predicted object: the whole r-z velocity field on the DNS grid)

quotes.text: Subsequently, the predicted flow field for the next sequence is recursively fed back into the model as the input for the subsequent step.

quotes.text: A distinctive alternative approach the authors adopt is the two-scale methodology (He 2018; Chen & He 2022). The method is to couple a locally embedded near-wall fine-mesh DNS block (or a small number of blocks) with a global coarser mesh domain.
The underlying wisdom promotes a hybrid approach to couple the near-wall modelled Reynold-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) part with the scale-resolving outer flow
quotes.location: Section 1.1 (relation to near-wall modelling; cites Larsson et al. 2015 and Bose & Park 2018)

quotes.text: The global under-resolved near-wall coarse-mesh region outside the local fine-mesh block is governed by the augmented flow governing equations with additional source terms.

the overall objective of the present work is to develop, validate and demonstrate a new approach to simulating TBL with equivalent accuracy to wall-resolved LES but at a much lower computational cost, manifested in terms of the mesh count–Re scaling.

The key working of the present two-scale method is that the solution of the under-resolved global inner coarse-mesh region will be corrected using the time-invariant source terms originated from the local fine-mesh blocks and propagated spatially by a block-spectral mapping.
The lower boundary is the no-slip wall.

independently_located_designs.source_reading: At Re_H=10595, DG SA RANS enriched 16×8 then 32×16 yields x_reatt/H 7.32→7.59. Separate resolved same-closure RANS benchmark gives 7.7, high-resolution LES gives 4.6–4.7. Refinement decreases error to the former and increases error to the latter. At 19000, 7.35→7.59 versus Rapp–Manhart experimental 4.21, again increasing physical-reference error. Cf/Cp reference curves appear for 10595 only (Fig. 8), while velocity references occur at both Re.
independently_located_designs.scientific_effect: Split two hill cases from the channel and name the reference per interpretation. Refinement tests numerical convergence of a RANS closure; only comparison to resolved LES/experiment tests physical discrepancy. Same enrichment on fine and coarse mesh.

quotes.text: The wall-functions are based on transfer of a boundary condition from a wall to some intermediate boundary near the wall (usually the first nearest to a wall mesh point but that is not obligatory).
To avoid direct resolution of the viscous sublayer, so-called high-Reynoldsnumber (HR) models have been developed. In this type of models the sublayer domain is not directly resolved.
Because of low velocities in the sublayer, models that resolve the sublayer are called low-Reynolds-number (LR) models.

observables.reading: All active treatments improve magnitude versus no-slip. Three active curves for magnitude nearly coincide. Direction profiles away from wall are similar even when wall-traction angles differ. The upstream profile is partly a setup target.

observables.quantity: Turning angle of mean surface traction relative to free stream
observables.benchmark: Schwarz & Bradshaw bent-duct measurements; output-dependent instruments, station support and errors.
observables.criterion: Magnitude of departure from measured centreline turning angle through bend.
observables.runs_and_controls: Coarse/fine EQWM, PDE and integral NEQWM along centreline. Compare active PDE vs EQWM on a single grid within bend.
observables.reading: PDE is closest, integral intermediate, equilibrium furthest in bend; maximum PDE–EQ difference about 5° at x′/L=.49. A poorer EQ direction is not evidence that adding a wall model worsened another quantity.

observables.quantity: Reynolds normal and shear stress profiles
observables.source_location: §3.4 Figs 13,14 (five stations); Fig. 15 for shear/gradient angles, pp. A29-19–20
observables.benchmark: Schwarz & Bradshaw bent-duct measurements; output-dependent instruments, station support and errors.
observables.criterion: Compare individual components, location and wall distance; outer stresses need not rank profiles near wall.
observables.runs_and_controls: Coarse EQWM, integral, PDE, and no-slip at stations 4,8,12,16,20 for stress components; stress/gradient angles at selected stations.
observables.reading: All active treatments improve normal and shear profiles over no-slip. Wall-parallel normal stresses agree better; wall-normal component is low near wall. Experiment misses inner peak locations. Some components can be both improved and still inaccurate.

observables.quantity: Boundary-layer thickness δ and momentum thickness θ
observables.benchmark: Schwarz & Bradshaw bent-duct measurements; output-dependent instruments, station support and errors.
observables.criterion: Agreement of thickness distributions with experiment; no common measured performance of no-slip here.
observables.runs_and_controls: All three active models on coarse grid, plotted along centreline in and around bend. Inflow iterated on the first measured station.
observables.reading: Reasonable agreement across cases; the three results are close. Do not turn this into a ranked wall-treatment improvement.

observables.quantity: Static pressure coefficient on floor, especially post-bend recovery
observables.benchmark: Schwarz & Bradshaw bent-duct measurements; output-dependent instruments, station support and errors.
observables.criterion: Downstream centreline C_p relative to reference pressure at x′=0, contrasted with bend pressure.
observables.runs_and_controls: Coarse EQWM pressure shown along multiple z′ lines; caption reports near-identical pressure from other active models/grids. Recovery experiments on centreline only.
observables.reading: Pressure agrees in most of bend; downstream predicted C_p relaxes to zero while experimental centreline stays slightly negative. Lengthening the computational duct did not remove discrepancy. No no-slip pressure curve for a shared-wall gain.

independently_located_designs.source_reading: Authors explicitly used already-trained models supplied by their originators in LESGO and did not retrain. BK22 was trained at Re_tau 2000, 4200 and 8000. The cited original tests extend to 10^6. The port tests up to 10^10, finding negative log-layer mismatch at that endpoint. Fig. 5’s only DNS profile is Re_tau=5200. High-Re profile mismatch is measured against the stated log law. ZYZY22 was already retrained in its original work with synthetic channel log-law data from 10^3 to 10^9. It requires .03 delta spacing and a 32^3 grid; BK22 and EWM/HYK19 use different matching/filter arrangements.
independently_located_designs.scientific_effect: Strong target-isolated transfer design for the frozen BK22 port beyond the original assessment when the stated endpoint is mismatch against the analytic law. A physical DNS-based profile claim at 10^10 lacks source support. Architecture ranking or port-versus-original comparisons across different meshes answer different questions. Figs. 12–13 separately compare prescribed channel inputs to a stitched Re_tau 5200 DNS/log-law reference.

disposition_settlement.reason: Disposition eligible under the published rule, without S1 to S3. Qualifying design: turbulent channel RANS at Re_H = 1e6 to 1e8 with the standard k-epsilon model and high-Re wall functions (first cell y+ about 50), whose u+ profile is plotted against the analytic law of the wall, Eq. (13), in Figs 2 and 4. This is 'a whole calculation using an identifiable wall treatment' (and a check of its imposed response) with values of calculation and comparator displayed. Eligibility does not depend on counting the adjoint wall function as a wall treatment; the rule does not say whether a boundary condition of the adjoint (sensitivity) equations is 'a named treatment', and that point is left open. The comparator is the same law the wall function imposes, so the design shows consistency, not independent validation. No fact is disputed between the readings.

quotes.text: Keywords: Adjoint Fluid Flow, Adjoint Law of the Wall, Adjoint Wall Functions, Adjoint Turbulence Modelling

They refer to standard approaches, used by most engineering finite volume methods, and employ a prescribed shear stress τw = τeff as well as pressure load on the wall face of the wall adjacent elements to close the primal momentum equations.
We thus use stress conditions and prescribe τ̂w = τ̂eff and p̂ instead of a simple Dirichlet condition û(y = 0) = ûw , which helps to match with the wall function (17).

A friction condition is used along the top and bottom boundaries in conjunction with low-Re and high-Re grids. The numerical grids consist of 4 × 250 finite volumes and the wall normal resolutions reach down to y + = O(10−1 ) for the low-Re cases and y + ≈ 50 for the high-Re cases.
Fig. 2 validates the compliance of both approaches for high-Re simulations over the normalised wall distance.
Figure 4 depicts the results obtained for the high-Re simulations. It is seen, that the log-layer branch of the two solutions (13) and (17) is again matched fairly accurate

disposition_settlement.reason: Disposition eligible under the published rule read with clarification S2 (a relation returning the wall shear stress from off-wall velocity, evaluated on DNS reference data, is 'a stress estimator' although the source presents it as reduced-order modelling); S3 is satisfied (Fig. 9 plot of prediction against actual stress; errors 18/22/about 100% and 28/30/120%). The rule does not decide without S2. Solver class of the qualifying design: prescribed input; no coupled calculation carries the estimator, so no first-cell spacing applies. Remaining point that S2 as written does not address: the estimator is a forecast (Delta T* = 25, upstream-shifted input, 500-1000 time lags), not a same-instant wall-stress relation. The readings do not disagree on any fact; the split into one or two prescribed-input designs and the listing or not of the opposition-control DNS (which tests no stress estimator) are row granularity.

quotes.text: 3.2. Reduced-order modelling: reconstruction of the wall-shear stress from 𝑢 We evaluate the predictive capabilities of the informative and residual components of the streamwise velocity fluctuations to reconstruct the wall shear stress in the future.

In the first case, we devise a model for the pointwise, temporal forecasting of 𝜏𝑥,+ using pointwise data of 𝑢. In the second scenario, the spatially two-dimensional wall-shear stress is reconstructed using 𝑢 data from a wall-parallel plane located at given distance from the wall.

The data are obtained from direct numerical simulation in a computational domain of size 8𝜋ℎ × 2ℎ × 4𝜋ℎ in the streamwise, wall-normal, and spanwise directions, respectively, where ℎ represents the channel half-height.
The Reynolds number, based on the friction velocity 𝑢 𝜏 , is Re 𝜏 = 𝑢 𝜏 ℎ/𝜈 ≈ 180.
The data is extracted from a simulation with the same set-up and friction Reynolds number as in §3 but in a smaller computational domain
The results indicate that the predictions based on 𝑢 and 𝑢˜ 𝐼 are comparable, with relative meansquared errors of 18% and 22%, respectively.

scope_boundary.kind: estimator not presented as a wall model
scope_boundary.basis: Disposition eligible under the published rule read with clarification S2 (a relation returning the wall shear stress from off-wall velocity, evaluated on DNS reference data, is 'a stress estimator' although the source presents it as reduced-order modelling); S3 is satisfied (Fig. 9 plot of prediction against actual stress; errors 18/22/about 100% and 28/30/120%). The rule does not decide without S2. Solver class of the qualifying design: prescribed input; no coupled calculation carries the estimator, so no first-cell spacing applies. Remaining point that S2 as written does not address: the estimator is a forecast (Delta T* = 25, upstream-shifted input, 500-1000 time lags), not a same-instant wall-stress relation. The readings do not disagree on any fact; the split into one or two prescribed-input designs and the listing or not of the opposition-control DNS (which tests no stress estimator) are row granularity.
